planting.note: Establish rooted offshoots in spring in deep, well-drained soil with full desert sun; this is one of Oman's latest-ripening varieties, so give it the longest possible hot season before harvest.

directions: Khasab is a late-maturing Omani cultivar grown mainly across the northern Batinah and Dakhiliyah plantations, where it is harvested as late as October, well behind the early varieties that finish by midsummer. The oval fruit ripens from light red on the tree to reddish-brown at the soft rutab stage and dark brown at full tamr cure, with a sweet, mildly astringent flesh and only moderate fiber. Because it holds lower total sugar than many other Omani cultivars, it is prized locally more as a premium fresh-eating and market date than as a dried storage date. Grow it like any Arabian date palm, giving it full sun, deep well-drained soil, and a long rainless summer to finish its unusually extended ripening window.
sources: Sultan Qaboos University College of Agricultural and Marine Sciences — Date Palm Status and Perspective in Oman
Oman Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources

planting.note: Establish rooted offshoots in spring in deep, well-drained soil with full desert sun; Nagal is one of Oman's earliest-ripening dates, reaching the fresh khalal stage by May.

directions: Nagal (also spelled Naghal) is among the most widely planted date cultivars in Oman, with hundreds of thousands of trees spread across nearly every growing region of the Sultanate, reflecting its reputation for dependable, heavy annual yields. It is an early-season cultivar, reaching the fresh, crunchy khalal stage by May, well ahead of the late-ripening varieties that finish in autumn. Like other Omani dates it should be grown from offshoots in deep, well-drained soil under intense, dry summer heat, since consistent high temperatures are what allow the fruit to cure properly on the tree. Its wide adaptability across Oman's different growing districts makes it a dependable backbone variety for growers who need reliable early fruit rather than a specialty or luxury date.
sources: Sultan Qaboos University College of Agricultural and Marine Sciences — Date Palm Status and Perspective in Oman
Oman Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources

planting.note: Establish rooted offshoots in spring in deep, well-drained soil with full desert sun; Zabad flowers in February and needs a long, hot season running into August before its luxury-grade rutab is ready.

directions: Zabad, whose name translates roughly as 'butter,' is regarded as one of the most luxurious of Oman's traditional date cultivars, prized above ordinary varieties for the exceptionally soft, rich texture of its rutab-stage fruit. It flowers in February and ripens late, through to August, giving growers in interior districts away from the humid coast a long, dry finishing season that this cultivar is specifically noted to reward. Propagate from offshoots into deep, well-drained soil in full sun exactly as with other Arabian dates, but site it where summer heat is reliable and dry, since Zabad's reputation rests on fruit quality that depends on a long uninterrupted ripening period rather than on heavy yield. It is grown in smaller quantities than Oman's major commercial varieties and traded more as a specialty table date than a bulk export crop.
sources: Sultan Qaboos University College of Agricultural and Marine Sciences — Date Palm Status and Perspective in Oman
Oman Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources

planting.note: Transplant seedlings into terraced, well-drained highland soil in filtered shade; like other Yemeni highland landraces it needs several years of steady care before its first harvest.

directions: Ismaili is a traditional Yemeni highland coffee landrace grown on the ancient rain-fed terraces around Bani Ismail, west of Sana'a, one of several morphologically distinct coffee populations identified in genetic surveys of Yemen's centuries-old coffee gardens. It is notable among Yemen's landraces for an unusually small, rounded, pea-shaped bean and a comparatively lighter, more delicate cup than the bolder, winey character typical of other Yemeni mountain coffees. Grow it exactly as you would any highland Arabica: dappled shade from taller companion trees, consistent but never waterlogged moisture, and patience, since cherries take three to four years to appear on young plants. Hand-harvested and traditionally dried whole in the cherry on stone terraces, it represents a genetic lineage largely separate from the Bourbon and Typica lines that spread from Yemen to the rest of the coffee-growing world.
sources: World Coffee Research — Yemeni Coffee Genetic Diversity
Sweet Maria's Coffee Library — Yemen Coffee Overview

planting.note: Transplant seedlings into terraced, well-drained mountain soil in filtered shade at high elevation; this landrace is adapted to some of the highest, coolest coffee terraces in Yemen.

directions: Khulani takes its name from the Khulan Amer district of Yemen's Sa'dah governorate, where it is grown on steep mountain terraces and in valley gardens at elevations reported between roughly 1,400 and 2,500 meters, among the highest coffee-growing sites in the country. This elevation and the region's cool nights are credited with the landrace's distinctive cup, often described as earthy with notes of caramel, banana, and dark chocolate, setting it apart from the brighter, winey profiles of Yemen's lower-elevation landraces. Cultivate it as you would other Yemeni highland Arabica: dappled shade, careful irrigation on terraced rainfed ground, and several years of growth before the first cherry harvest. As with Yemen's other ancient landraces, cherries are hand-picked and dried whole, and the plant's genetics are considered part of a lineage distinct from the Bourbon and Typica stock that colonized coffee farms worldwide.
sources: World Coffee Research — Yemeni Coffee Genetic Diversity
Sweet Maria's Coffee Library — Yemen Coffee Overview
